## Git basics — just enough to get going {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## What is Git, really?

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
Git tracks changes to a folder of files over time. Think of it as a
**save history** for your project — one you can rewind, compare, and,
crucially, **push to a server** so the world can see it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition — repository ("repo")
A folder that Git is tracking. It contains your files **and** the
full history of every change you've committed.
:::

We are going to use exactly four Git commands today. That's it — no
branching, no merging, no rebasing. Everything else can wait.

## The four commands you need today

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git init` | Start tracking a folder |
| `git add <file>` | Stage a file — mark it for the next commit |
| `git commit -m "message"` | Save a snapshot, with a note describing it |
| `git push` | Send your commits to GitHub |

::: {style="text-align: center; margin-top: 1em; font-size: 1.1em; color: #666;"}
Local folder → staged → committed → pushed to GitHub
:::

## A mental model

::: {style="font-size: 1.2em;"}
Think of `git add` + `git commit` as **taking a photograph** of your
project at this exact moment, with a caption explaining what changed.

`git push` **mails that photograph** to GitHub, where it becomes
visible to anyone with the link — including, in a few minutes, your
live website.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## A commit is not automatic
Git does not save your work continuously. If you don't `add` and
`commit`, your changes exist only on your laptop — and if you don't
`push`, GitHub never sees them. Committing often is a habit, not a
one-time step.
:::

## Create your repository {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## The one naming rule that matters today

::: {style="font-size: 1.3em; text-align: center; margin-top: 1em;"}
GitHub Pages will publish a personal site automatically **if, and
only if,** your repository is named exactly:
:::

::: {style="text-align: center; font-family: monospace; font-size: 1.6em; margin-top: 0.8em; color: #B87333;"}
yourusername.github.io
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## This has to match exactly
Replace `yourusername` with **your actual GitHub username**, all
lowercase, exactly as it appears on your GitHub profile. A mismatch
here is the single most common reason a site fails to deploy.
:::

## Steps: create the repo on GitHub

1. Go to **github.com** and click **New repository**
2. Repository name: `yourusername.github.io`
3. Visibility: **Public** — required for free GitHub Pages
4. Do **not** initialize with a README yet — we'll add our own later
5. Click **Create repository**

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why public?
Free GitHub Pages hosting requires a public repository. This is
fine — a professional website is *meant* to be public.
:::

## Choose your working folder

First, decide **where on your computer** this will live. Pick one
folder for all your course work if you don't already have one.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
cd ~\Documents\ECON5371
```

If the folder doesn't exist yet, create it first:

```powershell
mkdir ~\Documents\ECON5371
cd ~\Documents\ECON5371
```

### Mac / Linux

```bash
cd ~/Documents/ECON5371
```

If the folder doesn't exist yet, create it first:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/Documents/ECON5371
cd ~/Documents/ECON5371
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why this matters
`git clone` creates a new folder wherever your terminal is currently
"standing." If you don't `cd` somewhere deliberate first, you may end
up with your website folder buried inside Downloads or some other
random location — annoying to find later.
:::

## Clone it to your laptop

GitHub shows you a URL after creating the repo. Copy it, then run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/yourusername.github.io.git
cd yourusername.github.io
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 1em;"}
This creates a new folder named `yourusername.github.io` **inside**
whatever folder you were in — so `Documents/ECON5371/yourusername.github.io`,
following the example above. `clone` downloads an empty repo and
automatically connects it to GitHub — no separate `git init` needed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Keep track of this path
Positron will need to open this exact folder for the rest of the lab.
If you're not sure where you are, run `pwd` (Mac/Linux) or `cd` with
no arguments (Windows PowerShell) to print your current location.
:::

## Scaffold the site with Quarto {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## One command, a working site

From inside your cloned repo folder:

```bash
quarto create project website
```

Quarto will ask a few questions (directory — say **current
directory** since you're already inside your repo folder) and then
generate a starter website for you.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What just happened?
Quarto created a small set of files that together define a website:
a config file, a homepage, and an "about" page — plus a render
pipeline that turns your `.qmd` files into `.html` pages.
:::

## Tour of the generated files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `_quarto.yml` | Site-wide configuration — title, navigation, theme, output location |
| `index.qmd` | Your homepage |
| `about.qmd` | A starter "about" page — we'll repurpose this |
| `styles.css` | Optional custom styling |

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 1em;"}
Every page on your site starts as a `.qmd` file. Quarto renders each
one into HTML when you build the site.
:::

## Preview locally before you publish

```bash
quarto preview
```

This opens a live preview in your browser and **updates
automatically** as you save changes to any `.qmd` file — no need to
re-run the command after every edit.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Good habit
Keep the preview open in a browser tab while you build. You'll catch
formatting mistakes immediately instead of after deploying.
:::

## Build your pages {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Two pages, not five

::: {style="font-size: 1.2em;"}
Today we're keeping this simple: **one landing page** that holds
everything about you, and **one project page** that will grow into
your ECON-5371 research project over the semester.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why one page for everything?
A short academic site reads better as a single, well-organized page
than as five thin ones. You can always split sections out later —
Quarto makes that a five-minute change, not a rebuild.
:::

## Add pages to the navigation first

Before writing content, tell Quarto your pages exist. Open
`_quarto.yml` and add each page under `navbar`:

```yaml
website:
  title: "Your Name"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: project.qmd
        text: Project
```

Then create `project.qmd` — `index.qmd` already exists from the
scaffold.

## Page 1 — Home (`index.qmd`)

Everything about you lives here: intro, CV summary, research
interests, skills, and contact — in that order, using headings to
separate sections.

```markdown
---
title: "Your Name"
---

![](images/headshot.jpg){width=200px}

I am a graduate student in Economics at UTEP, studying
[your focus area].

## CV

[**Download full CV (PDF)**](files/cv.pdf)

**Education**

- M.S. Economics, University of Texas at El Paso (expected 20XX)
- B.A. Economics, [Institution] (20XX)

**Experience**

- [Role], [Organization], [Dates]

## Research interests

My research interests center on [topic area], particularly
[specific question or method].
```

## Page 1 — Home, continued

```markdown
## Skills

- Python (pandas, statsmodels, arch)
- R / Stata
- Git & GitHub
- Time series forecasting

## Contact

**Email:** your_email@miners.utep.edu

**LinkedIn:** [linkedin.com/in/yourname](https://linkedin.com/in/yourname) ·
**GitHub:** [github.com/yourusername](https://github.com/yourusername)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Save your headshot into an `images/` folder and your CV into a
`files/` folder, then reference each with the relative paths above.
:::

## Page 2 — Project (`project.qmd`)

A placeholder for now — analytical details are still ahead of you

```markdown
---
title: "Research Project"
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}

This page becomes the home for your paper, dashboard, and

## Configure for GitHub Pages {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Where does the site actually live?

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
GitHub Pages doesn't publish your `.qmd` files — it publishes
**rendered HTML**. Quarto needs to know where to put that HTML so
GitHub can find it.
:::

In `_quarto.yml`, confirm (or add) an output directory:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why `docs/`?
GitHub Pages can serve directly from a `/docs` folder on your `main`
branch — no separate deployment branch needed. This is the simplest
setup for a solo site.
:::

## The one invisible file that trips people up

Create an empty file named exactly `.nojekyll` inside your `docs/`
folder:

```bash
touch docs/.nojekyll
```

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Why this matters
GitHub Pages assumes Jekyll by default, which ignores files and
folders starting with an underscore — including Quarto's own output
folders. `.nojekyll` tells GitHub "don't do that." Skip this file and
parts of your site will silently fail to load.
:::

## Render the site

```bash
quarto render
```

This builds every `.qmd` file into HTML inside `docs/`. Run this
whenever you're ready to publish new changes — `quarto preview` is
for local editing only and does not update `docs/`.

## Turn on GitHub Pages (one-time setting)

On GitHub, in your repository:

1. Go to **Settings → Pages**
2. Under **Source**, select **Deploy from a branch**
3. Branch: **main** — Folder: **/docs**
4. Click **Save**

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 1em; color: #666;"}
You only need to do this once per repository.
:::

## Push and deploy {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Send it to GitHub

Back in the terminal, from your repo folder:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Initial website: home, CV, research, skills, contact"
git push
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; margin-top: 1em;"}
That's it. `git add .` stages every changed file, `commit` snapshots
them with a message, and `push` sends everything to GitHub.
:::

## Visit your site

Your site is live at:

::: {style="text-align: center; font-family: monospace; font-size: 1.5em; margin-top: 0.8em; color: #B87333;"}
https://yourusername.github.io
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Give it a few minutes
The first deploy can take 2–5 minutes to go live — GitHub is
building your site behind the scenes. If you see a 404, that's
usually why. Refresh in a bit before assuming something is broken.
:::

## Write your README.md {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Every repo tells you what it's for — or should

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
A `README.md` is the first thing anyone sees when they open your
repository — including you, six months from now. Today's version is
short, but the habit starts here. You'll write a fuller one for your
project repository later in the semester.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition — README
A Markdown file, always named `README.md`, placed at the root of a
repository. GitHub renders it automatically on the repo's front page.
:::

## What belongs in today's README

```markdown
# Your Name — Personal Website

Source code for my personal website, built with Quarto and
deployed via GitHub Pages.

**Live site:** https://yourusername.github.io

## Built with
- [Quarto](https://quarto.org)
- GitHub Pages

## Structure
- `index.qmd` — home page (CV, research interests, skills, contact)
- `project.qmd` — research project page
- `files/` — downloadable CV
- `images/` — headshot and other images
- `docs/` — rendered site (published output, do not edit directly)
```

## Commit the README

```bash
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git push
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 1em;"}
Refresh your repository page on GitHub — your README now renders
automatically below the file list.
:::

## If it's not working {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Common failure points, in order of likelihood

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| 404 at `yourusername.github.io` | Repo name doesn't exactly match `yourusername.github.io` |
| Site loads but looks broken/unstyled | Missing `.nojekyll` in `docs/` |
| Nothing published at all | Pages not enabled in **Settings → Pages**, or wrong branch/folder selected |
| Changes don't appear | Forgot `quarto render` before `git push` — you pushed source, not the rendered site |
| `git push` rejected | Repo has commits you don't have locally — ask for help before force-pushing anything |

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The fix is almost always: render, then push
The single most common gap is editing a `.qmd` file, forgetting to
run `quarto render`, and pushing stale HTML. Make "render → add →
commit → push" a fixed sequence.
:::

## Key Terms {.callout-note icon=false}

**Repository (repo)**
: A folder tracked by Git, containing files and their full change history.

**Commit**
: A saved snapshot of your project at a point in time, with a message describing the change.

**Push**
: Sending local commits to a remote server (GitHub).

**Clone**
: Downloading a copy of a remote repository to your local machine, pre-connected to that remote.

**GitHub Pages**
: A free hosting service that publishes static HTML directly from a GitHub repository.

**`.nojekyll`**
: An empty marker file that disables GitHub's default Jekyll processing, required for Quarto sites.

**README.md**
: A Markdown file at a repository's root, automatically rendered on the repo's GitHub page, describing what the project is and how to use it.

## Make it yours {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Today's site is the minimum — not the ceiling

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
A live, deployed site with your CV, research interests, skills, and
contact info **already satisfies today's requirement.** Everything
on the next few slides is optional exploration — worth doing, but
not another deadline. Don't spend three hours picking a font instead
of finishing a problem set.
:::

## Get inspiration

Browse a few academic and professional personal sites and note what
you like — layout, tone, what they choose to highlight first.
Borrowing structure is normal; nobody expects total originality from
a first website.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A reference, not a bar to clear
You're welcome to look at my own site's repository for ideas:

**[github.com/ncachanosky/website-quarto](https://github.com/ncachanosky/website-quarto)**

Mine is more customized than what you built today — that's expected
after years of iterating on it, not the standard for this week.
:::

## Styling — color

Two directions worth trying:

- **UTEP colors** — orange `#FF8200` and blue `#041E42`, if you want
  an institutional look
- **Your own palette** — pick 2–3 colors that feel like you; a
  simple approach is one accent color plus a neutral background and
  dark text

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Check contrast, not just taste
Light gray text on a white background looks clean but can be hard to
read. Aim for dark text on a light background (or the reverse) —
your eyes will thank you, and so will anyone with low vision.
:::

## Styling — typography

- Pick one font for body text and, optionally, a second for
  headings — more than two starts to look busy
- Body text should be comfortably readable at a normal zoom level;
  when in doubt, go slightly larger rather than smaller
- Quarto/reveal and website themes both support custom fonts via
  `_quarto.yml` or `styles.css` — small changes, visible impact

## Styling — favicon

That small icon in a browser tab is a **favicon**, and adding one is
a quick way to make your site feel finished rather than default.

```yaml
website:
  favicon: images/favicon.png
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
A square image (e.g., your initials, a simple mark, or even a small
version of your headshot) works well. Free favicon generators can
resize an image to the right dimensions if you don't want to do it
by hand.
:::

## Check it beyond your laptop screen

- **View it on your phone.** A common first-site issue is an image
  or table that looks fine on a laptop but overflows on a narrow
  screen — worth a quick check before calling it done.
- **Add alt text to your headshot** (and any other images):
  `![Alt text describing the image](images/headshot.jpg)`. It helps
  screen-reader users and costs you one sentence.

## Optional, advanced: a custom domain

If you already own a personal domain (or plan to), GitHub Pages can
serve your site from it instead of `yourusername.github.io`. This is
entirely optional and easy to add later — not something to set up
today.

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 1em; color: #666;"}
See GitHub's docs on "Managing a custom domain for your GitHub Pages
site" when you're ready.
:::

## Use AI tools to help

Claude, Copilot, and similar tools are well-suited to exactly this
kind of styling work. Some things worth trying:

- *"Here's my `styles.css` — help me change the accent color to a
  warm terracotta."*
- *"My headshot image is overflowing on mobile — here's my
  `index.qmd`, how do I fix the sizing?"*
- *"Suggest a font pairing for an academic personal website that
  feels modern but not flashy."*

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Paste in context, not just a question
Sharing the actual file (your `.qmd`, `.yml`, or `.css`) gets a far
more useful answer than describing the problem in the abstract — the
tool can point to the exact line to change.
:::
